preamble: A direct shift of the labiodental [f] to the alveolar sibilant [s] is very rare. The best-known case is word-initial fn- becoming sn- in Middle English, which turned earlier fnesen into snesen 'sneeze', fnoren into snoren 'snore' and fnorten into snorten 'snort'; the fn- forms fell out of use in the 1400s. The change can be read as place assimilation of [f] to the following alveolar [n], but some scholars attribute it to a misreading of the unfamiliar fn- as ſn- (sn- with a long s), so its status as a purely phonetic change is debated.

examples.from: fnesen (Middle English), from Old English fnēosan
examples.note: Initial fn- became sn-; a competing explanation attributes the change to misreading fn- as ſn- (long s).

examples.from: fnora 'snort, sneezing' (Old English), Middle English fnoren
examples.note: Same initial fn- > sn- change, which shows it was regular rather than a one-word accident.
